analysis.one_liner: Requires factories to treat or dispose of their hazardous waste on-site instead of shipping it away.
analysis.headline: A one-section bill requiring hazardous waste generators to treat, dispose of, or recycle waste where it was produced attracted 4 cosponsors, never got a hearing, and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every large hazardous waste generator — mostly chemical plants and manufacturers — to treat its waste until harmless, or dispose of or recycle it, at the site where the waste was created, instead of trucking it to a commercial landfill or incinerator elsewhere. Small-quantity generators would be exempt. The bill was a single section with no funding, no monitoring rules, and no standards for on-site disposal; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its hazardous materials subcommittee and never taken up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities along hazardous waste transport routes and near the handful of commercial disposal landfills and incinerators — often lower-income areas that receive other regions' waste — would no longer receive waste shipped from out of state, since the waste would have to stay where it was made. Residents near industrial plants could also benefit if on-site treatment actually rendered waste harmless there rather than letting it leave as an untracked liability.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near waste routes and landfills

how_it_helps.text: It would end the practice of hauling hazardous waste long distances to a small number of commercial disposal sites, keeping each generator's waste at its point of origin.
It requires treatment that renders the waste harmless before on-site disposal, a stricter standard than simply moving it off the property.
Businesses generating waste only in small quantities — the exemption tracks the small-quantity generator category in the Solid Waste Disposal Act — would not bear new on-site handling obligations.

analysis.who_pays: Industrial hazardous waste generators — chemical plants, manufacturers, and other factories that today ship waste off-site — would have to build and operate their own treatment or disposal capability on their property, a large capital and operating cost that would likely be passed to customers. Commercial waste haulers, landfills, and incinerator operators would lose the off-site disposal business the bill eliminates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical plants and commercial waste haulers

drawbacks.text: Every large generator would become its own disposal site: instead of waste concentrated at a few heavily watched commercial facilities, thousands of individual plants would each be treating or disposing of waste on their own property, with no new monitoring, permitting, or enforcement standards added to cover the shift.

The small-quantity generator exemption would leave a large class of businesses — all those under the Solid Waste Disposal Act's small-quantity threshold — free to keep sending waste off-site, creating an uneven system in which only large facilities are covered.
On-site treatment 'so as to render the waste harmless' may be technically or economically impossible for many generators, and the bill contains no mechanism, funding, or phase-in to help them comply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea addresses a real concern — hazardous waste traveling by truck and rail, and a few communities disproportionately hosting the nation's disposal sites — but as written the bill is a one-sentence mandate, not a workable law. It sets no standards for on-site treatment or disposal, provides no oversight or funding, and its small-generator exemption opens a sizable loophole. Honest supporters would have to acknowledge that scattering disposal across thousands of industrial sites could create new local risks even as it removed waste from transport corridors. It was closer to a statement of principle than a design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its hazardous materials subcommittee, and nobody acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Kolter introduced the bill on September 26, 1990, in the final months of the 101st Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On October 8, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials, where it sat; no hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed.
The bill drew 4 cosponsors — 3 Democrats and 1 Republican — and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, without ever leaving committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial hazardous waste haulers, landfill operators, and industrial generators that prefer shipping waste off-site are better off, because no new on-site mandate was ever imposed; the communities the bill aimed to protect got nothing.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; the bill never gained broader support.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing or markup; it was sent to a subcommittee on October 8, 1990, and no action followed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 4 cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 1 Republican, but with no hearings or votes there is no record of where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Commercial hazardous waste disposal, hauling, and incineration
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated their core market by barring generators from shipping waste off-site. Their loss would have been a gain for communities along transport routes, though these regulated facilities also handle waste that individual factories cannot safely manage themselves.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and other industrial waste generators
industries.note: They would have had to build and run on-site treatment or disposal instead of paying a hauler, a major cost. Their preference for the cheaper off-site option ran directly against the bill's protective aim.

The bill exempted generators below the Solid Waste Disposal Act's small-quantity threshold, letting them keep using the commercial disposal system their larger competitors could no longer use — and continuing to send waste into the transport and disposal system the bill aimed to shut down.
